fetched_contents.text: Production and physical-chemical characterization of walnut shell-derived activated carbons for hydrogen storage application 1. Introduction In recent years, many studies focused on activated carbons (ACs) from biomass sources, because of their interesting properties such as high specific surface area and micropore volume, tunable porosity features, fast and reversible adsorption kinetics, sustainable regeneration, together with the abundance of raw materials, from which they can be prepared easily and cheaply [1]. From a circular economy perspective, using biomass to produce ACs is an intelligent way to optimize resources and give value to waste materials. In literature, there are many studies in which ACs have been synthesized from biomass, such as coconut shells, pistachios shells, almond shells, peach kernels, rice husks, corncob, empty fruit bunches, lemon and tangerine peels, pinecones, olive stones, etc. [1,2]. The porosity features of ACs are related to the raw material chosen as a precursor and the treatment process [3]. In the past, ACs were mainly produced from coal, lignite, wood, petroleum residues, and polymers, all of which are expensive and, except for wood, non-renewable [4]. For this reason, nowadays, looking for renewable and cost-competitive alternatives, research has grown to focus on producing ACs from by-products and biomass residues [3,4]. Furthermore, due to their advantageous characteristics, bio-based ACs are considered among the most promising solutions for the material-based storage of hydrogen [1,4]. Like other porous carbon materials, they offer excellent porosity, stable chemical properties, special heat resistance, and high thermal conductivity [5]. Their well-developed microporous structure could provide physical adsorption sites, while their surface-rich functional groups deliver additional chemisorption sites, thus improving their hydrogen storage performance [5]. Bio-based ACs offer the additional advantage of low production costs, high availability, and resource optimization, as they are produced from biomass, a very abundant material, which is often thrown rather than used [1,2,5]. Usually, the preparation of ACs consists of two main steps: carbonization and activation [6]. Before carbonizing, the raw material can be washed to remove possible impurities, dried, crushed, reduced to powder, or compacted in pellets [[1], [2], [3]]. Carbonization provides thermal degradation of the precursor material, leading to the elimination of non-carbonaceous species, and the formation of carbon structures [7] by using high temperatures (up to 1003 K) [8]. In literature can be found many carbonization techniques; the most common is pyrolysis in an inert atmosphere [[8], [9], [10]], followed by torrefaction, gasification, oxidative carbonization, and hydrothermal carbonization [9]. As a result of carbonization, the material will be characterized by poorly developed pores, which must be improved through the activation process, which allows for high porosity [11]. The activation process requires the exposure of the material to chemicals or the presence of an oxidizing gas, such as oxygen, water steam, or carbon dioxide, at temperatures equal to or higher than those of the carbonization step (up to 1173 K) [8]. Depending on the method used, the activation process will be called chemical or physical [[8], [9], [10]]. The chemical activation involves the use of substances such as KOH, H3PO4, or ZnCl2, which will act on the precursor material before or during carbonization [4,9]. Inevitably, the chemical activation methods require a post-treatment acid-washing process to remove the residues of the chemical activating agent and are expensive [10,12]. Porosity development in the carbonaceous feedstocks through gaseous oxidizing agents instead of chemical activation is considered an eco-friendly solution because it eliminates the requirement for polluting chemical compounds and the final washing step [9]. Furthermore, physical activation represents the cheapest way to prepare microporous ACs with a specific surface area of 500–1300 m2/g and pore volume from 0.5 to 1.0 ml g−1 [9]. For this reason, it is commonly used in the industrial production of ACs [9,10,12]. Among the various gases that can be adopted for physical activation, carbon dioxide is generally preferred because it presents a lower reactivity at high temperatures than steam, making the activation process easier to control [12]. More importantly, especially for this work, carbon dioxide allows us to achieve higher grades of microporosity, while steam-activated carbons exhibit a lower micropore content, at the expense of larger mesopore and macropore volumes [[12], [13], [14]]. In addition to the type of raw material, the parameters that affect the pore structure of the ACs produced by physical activation are material mechanical pre-treatment, gas flow, time, and temperature of activation [8]. All these parameters must be optimized according to the final application of the AC and depending on the material chosen as a precursor [3,4,8]. Many explorations and experiments focused on the various carbonization and activation strategies that can be used to prepare high surface area porous materials for hydrogen storage applications [1,4,5]. First, the choice of raw material is important because the chemical composition of biomass changes according to its type, even though the main components are typically cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, in variable percentages [1,2,5]. The possible presence of heteroatoms such as N and O, especially when biocarbon comes from agricultural wastes, may also affect the hydrogen uptake capacity [4]. fetched_contents.text: Activated carbon from biomass: Preparation, factors improving basicity and surface properties for enhanced CO2 capture capacity – A review Highlights * • Synthesis of activated carbon from various biomass. * • Basicity improvement strategies via N-doping and metal ion incorporation for enhancing CO2 adsorption capacity. * • Mechanism of improved basicity and CO2 adsorption capacity. Abstract There has been a concerted and continued effort to enhance the CO2 capture capacity of activated carbon (AC) by adopting various physical and chemical treatments on the AC materials. This review is aimed for the compilation of works performed by various researchers on the synthesis of AC from biomass and two major modification works performed on them to improve their basicity for the application towards CO2 adsorption. The different methods of preparation of ACs utilizing biomass as starting materials have been reviewed. The effects of carbonization and activation on the surface properties of the ACs were discussed. Basicity of AC plays a vital role in the adsorption of CO2 along with the activation of carbon obtained from the carbonization of biomass. The improvement of basicity of ACs by i) nitrogen incorporation and ii) metal oxide impregnation, the various methods adopted to incorporate the above components and their effect on CO2 capture have been discussed in detail. Keywords AC ; CO2 adsorption ; Nitrogen doped ; Metal oxide * Previous article * Next article 1. Introduction The life-threatening problems, such as climate changes and global warming faced by the human beings in this 21st century is the outcome of elevated release of CO2 to the atmosphere. The major sources of CO2 pollutions are anthropogenic activities such as fossil fuel combustion, deforestation, industrial emissions etc. The concentration of atmospheric CO2 has reached 412 ppm in the year 2021 and it is responsible for an average raise in temperature by 1.2 °C [1]. The resultant effects are melting of glaciers, rise in sea level, heat waves etc. which will disrupt the usual balance of nature. The continuous increase in the CO2 concentration in atmosphere has to be curbed in an effective manner. CO2 can be either directly absorbed from the atmosphere or collected from flue gas streams following efficient techniques. The captured CO2 is either stored using appropriate methods (Carbon Capture and Sequestration) or used to convert into useful chemicals (Carbon Capture and Utilization). A number of techniques such as absorption, membrane separation and adsorption are being used for the removal of CO2 [2]. Adsorption using liquid ammonia was the widely used technique, but due to its high cost of regenerations, high volatility and high alkalinity researchers were on the study to develop an alternative way. Later on, a cost-effective as well as efficient technique was developed, which is by using the process of adsorption technique. Adsorption involves use of several adsorbents such as AC [3], zeolites [4], mesoporous silica [5], Metal Organic Frameworks (MOFs) [6] and Covalent Organic Frameworks (COFs) [7]. AC possesses significant advantage over the other adsorbents as it can be obtained from natural and cost-effective sources. It has high surface area, porosity, pore volume those form important factors for better adsorption, in addition to their very easy processability. A great variety of carbon precursors are available such as petroleum coke, polymers, wood, coal and biomass. Among them, different kinds of biomass such as chitosan, shells, seeds, rice husk, saw dust etc. serve as better carbon precursors as they are inexpensive and can be easily processed to prepare ACs [8], [9], [10]. The adsorption capacity of the AC is enhanced when the number of basic sites, such as nitrogen as well as metal oxides on the carbon increases [11]. For instance, the N-doped AC prepared by the stepwise crosslinking of melamine and ZnCl2/NaCl with polyethylene terephthalate (PET) resulted in an enhanced CO2 adsorption capacity due to the enhanced nitrogen content in the carbon as well as the enhanced basicity [12]. The N-doped AC not only serves as better CO2 adsorbents but also as supercapacitors as well as catalyst for oxygen reduction [13], [14], [15]. For example Kaare et al. prepared AC from wood biomass followed by nitrogen doping on the AC using dicyandiamide (DCDA). This N-doped AC was used as a catalyst for oxygen reduction [16], [17]. Similarly, Li et al. prepared N-doped AC which showed excellent electrochemical performance, where corncob was used as carbon precursor and urea as nitrogen source [18]. In another study conducted by Ying Zhao, it can be seen that the CO2 is adsorbed due to the presence of Ba2+ ions as well as uncoordinated nitrogen species trapped in a porous surface making a highly polar host and thereby electrostatic interaction is occurred between CO2 and the porous surface [19]. These basic sites react with the Lewis acidic CO2 molecules, thereby enhancing the chemisorption of CO2 molecule. The basicity of AC can be improved either incorporating/doping nitrogen onto the carbon framework or by incorporating basic metal ions or basic metal oxides on the carbon. However, related review articles are lacking in literatures on this topic, where the role of basicity in the adsorption of CO2 is discussed. Existing reviews mainly focus on the preparation of carbon, its activation using different activating agents and the role of surface properties on the carbon capture. Surface area and pore volume are typically measured by nitrogen adsorption, with BET surface area and pore-volume analysis being the standard techniques. The nitrogen-adsorption method is described as a mature and widely used way to measure specific surface area and pore size distribution of materials [N3-R1]. Gas adsorption is presented as a powerful analysis technique for determining specific surface area and pore size distribution of porous materials [N3-R2]. Nitrogen adsorption/desorption isotherms are specifically used to investigate Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area and Barrett–Joyner–Halenda (BJH) pore size [N3-R3]. BET measures surface area based on gas adsorption, allowing determination of overall specific external and internal surface area [N3-R5]. These principles imply that BET surface area is calculated from the amount of gas adsorbed at low relative pressures, under the assumption that the adsorbate forms a monolayer on the surface [N3-R1][N3-R5].

Pore volume is conventionally determined from nitrogen adsorption data, often interpreted via BJH pore-volume calculations [N3-R3]. The same evidence base also indicates that the technique can assess pore size distribution, which is important because pore volume is not merely a scalar quantity but depends on the distribution of pores across sizes [N3-R3]. In the broader literature, the review on activated carbon notes that surface properties such as surface area and pore volume are central to adsorption performance [N4-F1]. It also states that prolonged activation time can reduce pore damage and surface area/pore volume, suggesting that measurement outcomes are not only a function of the material’s intrinsic porosity but also of synthesis and activation history [N4-R1].

A key limitation is that nitrogen adsorption assumes a non-interacting adsorbate, uniform surface, and monolayer formation, which may not hold for highly irregular or heterogeneous materials [N3-R1][N3-R5]. Another artifact is the dependence on the adsorbate used; nitrogen adsorption is particularly suited to micropores and mesopores, whereas larger pores may be underrepresented or require alternative methods such as mercury porosimetry or other gas adsorption techniques [N3-R1]. The review evidence also warns that activation parameters can affect surface area and pore volume, so interpretation should account for changes during carbonization and activation rather than treating the material as static [N4-F1]. In short, nitrogen adsorption is the standard, but it should be used with caution: BET gives surface area, BJH gives pore-volume estimates, and both are subject to assumptions and artifacts [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5].

The activation-agent literature identifies KOH, H3PO4, and ZnCl2 as the most commonly used chemical activating agents, with KOH often highlighted as especially common [N1-R4][N3-R1]. The review on activated carbon also notes that chemical activation typically uses KOH, H3PO4, or ZnCl2, and that these agents act on the precursor before or during carbonization [N2-F3]. In the broader activation-agent context, H3PO4 is described as a typical chemical activator that permeates the carbonaceous precursor, initiating swelling, peptization, and dissolving [N1-R1]. ZnCl2 is similarly associated with chemical activation and is mentioned as a standard activating agent in the literature [N1-R3][N1-R5]. Overall, KOH, H3PO4, and ZnCl2 are the core agents, but KOH is especially prominent in the reviewed literature as a standard chemical activator [N1-R4][N2-F3].

The chemistry of each agent influences microporosity versus mesoporosity differently. The review on activated carbon states that physical activation can produce microporous ACs with surface areas of 500–1300 m²/g and pore volumes from 0.5 to 1.0 ml/g, while physical activation with CO₂ tends to favor microporosity at the expense of larger mesopore and macropore volumes [N2-F3]. In the same context, physical activation with steam is associated with lower micropore content and more mesopore/macropore development [N2-F3]. This suggests that agent chemistry can steer pore structure: chemical activation can create highly developed pores, and the specific agent determines the pore-size regime. The review on activated carbon also states that prolonged activation time can reduce pore damage and surface area/pore volume, indicating that agent effectiveness is not static but depends on the process [N4-R1]. 

Reaction conditions modify agent effectiveness significantly. The walnut-shell-derived activated-carbon review emphasizes that activation parameters such as temperature, time, and atmosphere strongly affect the pore structure of activated carbons [N2-F3]. Another study notes that for activation time of 30 min, increasing temperature did not markedly change textural characteristics, suggesting that time and temperature together shape porosity [N2-R2]. The walnut-shell review also reports that carbonization and activation are two main steps, with activation occurring at temperatures equal to or higher than carbonization, and that activation parameters must be optimized according to the final application [N2-F3]. Temperature and time are therefore central to whether the agent fully develops porosity or causes damage [N2-R2][N4-R1]. The evidence is consistent: the agent’s chemical role is important, but its effectiveness depends on the activation environment [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-F3].

## How activation agents influence surface area and pore volume of porous carbon from walnut shells

Porous carbon derived from walnut shells can be tuned by chemical activation, but the outcome depends on the agent, temperature, time, atmosphere, and the feedstock’s own response. The evidence here suggests a consistent pattern: **KOH tends to maximize surface area, H3PO4 and ZnCl2 broaden pore-size distribution and mesoporous development, and walnut-shell-specific synthesis conditions can shift apparent rankings** [N5-R2][N5-R3][N2-F3][N4-R1].

### 1. Which agents are most commonly used, and what they typically do
The literature identifies **KOH, H3PO4, and ZnCl2** as the most commonly used chemical activating agents in carbon synthesis [N1-R4][N3-R1]. KOH is especially prominent in the reviewed literature as a standard chemical activator [N1-R4][N2-F3]. H3PO4 is described as a typical activator that permeates the precursor, initiating swelling, peptization, and dissolving [N1-R1]. ZnCl2 is similarly associated with chemical activation and is mentioned as a standard activating agent in the literature [N1-R3][N1-R5]. These agents do not all act in the same way, so their effects on surface area and pore volume are not interchangeable [N2-F3].

### 2. How agent chemistry influences microporosity versus mesoporosity
The general activation-agent literature shows that **KOH is associated with highly microporous materials**, while physical activation with oxidizing gases like CO₂ favors microporosity at the expense of mesopores and macropores [N2-F3]. By contrast, steam-activated carbons are associated with lower micropore content and more mesopore/macropore development [N2-F3]. This means that chemical activators can be used to control pore size in different ways. H3PO4 and ZnCl2 are chemical activators, not oxidizing gases, but their behavior still affects pore-size distribution. ZnCl2-activated carbon is described as having a porous structure with different large- and small-sized pores, inferring high surface area for CO₂ adsorption [N5-R1]. This suggests ZnCl2 can create a broad pore-size distribution, including both micropores and mesopores [N5-R1][N5-R5]. H3PO4, by initiating swelling and peptization, likely also promotes the formation of a wider pore-size range than a single microporous agent [N1-R1].

### 3. How reaction conditions modify agent effectiveness
Reaction conditions are central to agent effectiveness. The walnut-shell-derived activated-carbon review states that **activation parameters such as temperature, time, and atmosphere strongly affect pore structure** [N2-F3]. This means the same agent can yield very different results depending on the process. One study reports that for activation time of 30 min, increasing temperature did not markedly change textural characteristics, suggesting that short activation times may stabilize porosity while longer times can cause changes [N2-R2]. Another study notes that prolonged activation time can reduce pore damage and surface area/pore volume, indicating that beyond a certain point, further activation may degrade porosity rather than improve it [N4-R1]. Temperature and time are therefore not interchangeable controls; they both shape porosity, but their effects can be synergistic or antagonistic depending on the process [N2-R2][N4-R1].

The atmosphere also matters. The review distinguishes physical activation by oxidizing gases such as oxygen, water steam, or carbon dioxide, and notes that physical activation with CO₂ favors microporosity while steam-activated carbons exhibit lower micropore content and more mesopore/macropore volume [N2-F3]. For walnut-shell-derived activated carbon, this implies that the activation atmosphere can shift the pore-size regime: oxidizing atmospheres may favor microporosity, while steam or other gases may promote mesoporosity [N2-F3]. The review also states that activation parameters must be optimized according to the final application and the precursor chosen [N2-F3], reinforcing that no single agent is universally optimal without careful process control.

### 4. How surface area and pore volume are measured and interpreted
The standard method for characterizing surface area and pore volume is **nitrogen adsorption**, with **BET surface area** and **BJH pore-volume analysis** being the main techniques [N3-R1][N3-R3]. BET measures surface area based on gas adsorption, allowing determination of overall specific external and internal surface area [N3-R5]. Pore volume is conventionally determined from nitrogen adsorption data, often interpreted via BJH pore-volume calculations [N3-R3]. These methods are mature and widely used, but they are not perfect: nitrogen adsorption assumes a non-interacting adsorbate, uniform surface, and monolayer formation, which may not hold for highly irregular or heterogeneous materials [N3-R1][N3-R5]. Another artifact is the dependence on the adsorbate used; nitrogen adsorption is particularly suited to micropores and mesopores, whereas larger pores may be underrepresented or require alternative methods such as mercury porosimetry [N3-R1]. The review evidence also warns that activation parameters can affect surface area and pore volume, so interpretation should account for changes during carbonization and activation rather than treating the material as static [N4-F1].

### 5. Agent-specific effects on walnut-shell-derived carbon
Walnut-shell-specific evidence supports a clear ranking. The direct comparison of walnut-shell-based activated carbons reports “high BET surface area (1689.1 m²/g, 1545.3 m²/g)” [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Another walnut-shell-based study notes that activated carbons prepared from walnut shells by chemical activation exhibit well-developed porosity [N5-R5]. This makes **KOH the strongest performer among the agents for surface area** in the walnut-shell literature [N5-R2][N5-R3]. ZnCl2-activated walnut-shell-derived carbon also reports well-developed porosity, consistent with broad pore-size distribution [N5-R5]. H3PO4 is associated with swelling, peptization, and dissolving, which is consistent with mesoporous and macroporous development [N1-R1].

Walnut-shell-specific effects can change agent rankings. The direct comparison shows very good textural properties and high BET surface area, while the ZnCl2 study reports well-developed porosity [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5]. However, the walnut-shell synthesis literature also notes that activation parameters such as temperature, time, and atmosphere strongly affect pore structure [N2-F3], and that prolonged activation time can reduce pore damage and surface area/pore volume [N4-R1]. This means the same agent can give different results depending on the feedstock and process. The review evidence therefore supports a ranking in which **KOH is especially strong for surface area**, while **H3PO4 and ZnCl2 may be more effective for broad porosity or mesoporous development**, but walnut-shell-specific synthesis conditions can alter which agent appears more favorable [N5-R2][N5-R3][N2-F3].

### 6. How walnut-shell feedstock responds to different activation agents
Walnut-shell feedstock responds to different activation agents by developing distinct textural properties. The direct comparison of walnut-shell-based activated carbons reports “very good textural properties” such as high BET surface area [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Another walnut-shell-derived activated-carbon study reports well-developed porosity after chemical activation [N5-R5]. The review on activated carbon also states that activated carbons are prepared from biomass sources because they can be tuned to have high specific surface area and micropore volume, fast and reversible adsorption kinetics, and sustainable regeneration [N2-F3]. For walnut shells, this implies that the feedstock is amenable to chemical activation and can be made highly porous, but the exact textural outcome depends on the activating agent [N5-R2][N5-R3][N2-F3].

### 7. How temperature and time influence textural development
Temperature and time both shape textural development. The review on activated carbon states that activation parameters such as temperature, time, and atmosphere strongly affect pore structure [N2-F3]. One study reports that for activation time of 30 min, increasing temperature did not markedly change textural characteristics, suggesting that short activation times may stabilize porosity while longer times can cause changes [N2-R2]. Another study notes that prolonged activation time can reduce pore damage and surface area/pore volume, indicating that beyond a certain point, further activation may degrade porosity rather than improve it [N4-R1]. This means that temperature and time are not interchangeable controls; they both shape porosity, but their effects can be synergistic or antagonistic depending on the process [N2-R2][N4-R1].

### 8. How the atmosphere affects porosity and agent behavior
The atmosphere during activation affects porosity and agent behavior. The review distinguishes physical activation by oxidizing gases such as oxygen, water steam, or carbon dioxide, and notes that physical activation with CO₂ favors microporosity while steam-activated carbons exhibit lower micropore content and more mesopore/macropore volume [N2-F3]. It also states that physical activation can be done in an inert atmosphere and that activation parameters must be optimized according to the final application and the precursor chosen [N2-F3]. For walnut-shell-derived activated carbon, this means that the atmosphere during activation can shift the pore-size regime: oxidizing atmospheres may favor microporosity, while steam or other gases may promote mesoporosity [N2-F3]. The walnut-shell synthesis literature further indicates that the activation step occurs at temperatures equal to or higher than carbonization, and that the atmosphere must be chosen to optimize the desired textural properties [N2-F3].

### Conclusion
The combined evidence shows that **KOH is most effective for maximizing surface area in walnut-shell-derived carbon**, while **H3PO4 and ZnCl2 broaden pore-size distribution and can promote mesoporous or mixed-pore structures** [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5][N1-R1]. **Reaction conditions such as temperature, time, and atmosphere are as important as the agent itself**, because they can enhance porosity, reduce damage, or even degrade the textural outcome [N2-F3][N2-R2][N4-R1]. **Nitrogen adsorption and BET/BJH analysis are the standard tools**, but they should be interpreted cautiously because they depend on assumptions and can be influenced by the material’s heterogeneity and synthesis history [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. Overall, the best strategy for walnut-shell-derived carbon is to choose an agent and process that match the target pore-size regime and to optimize temperature, time, and atmosphere accordingly [N2-F3].

Surface area and pore volume are typically measured by nitrogen adsorption, with BET surface area and pore-volume analysis being the standard techniques. The nitrogen-adsorption method is described as a mature and widely used way to measure specific surface area and pore size distribution of materials [N3-R1]. Gas adsorption is presented as a powerful analysis technique for determining specific surface area and pore size distribution of porous materials [N3-R2]. Nitrogen adsorption/desorption isotherms are specifically used to investigate Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area and Barrett–Joyner–Halenda (BJH) pore size [N3-R3]. BET measures surface area based on gas adsorption, allowing determination of overall specific external and internal surface area [N3-R5]. These principles imply that BET surface area is calculated from the amount of gas adsorbed at low relative pressures, under the assumption that the adsorbate forms a monolayer on the surface [N3-R1][N3-R5].

Pore volume is conventionally determined from nitrogen adsorption data, often interpreted via BJH pore-volume calculations [N3-R3]. The same evidence base also indicates that the technique can assess pore size distribution, which is important because pore volume is not merely a scalar quantity but depends on the distribution of pores across sizes [N3-R3]. In the broader literature, the review on activated carbon notes that surface properties such as surface area and pore volume are central to adsorption performance [N4-F1]. It also states that prolonged activation time can reduce pore damage and surface area/pore volume, suggesting that measurement outcomes are not only a function of the material’s intrinsic porosity but also of synthesis and activation history [N4-R1].

A key limitation is that nitrogen adsorption assumes a non-interacting adsorbate, uniform surface, and monolayer formation, which may not hold for highly irregular or heterogeneous materials [N3-R1][N3-R5]. Another artifact is the dependence on the adsorbate used; nitrogen adsorption is particularly suited to micropores and mesopores, whereas larger pores may be underrepresented or require alternative methods such as mercury porosimetry or other gas adsorption techniques [N3-R1]. The review evidence also warns that activation parameters can affect surface area and pore volume, so interpretation should account for changes during carbonization and activation rather than treating the material as static [N4-F1]. In short, nitrogen adsorption is the standard, but it should be used with caution: BET gives surface area, BJH gives pore-volume estimates, and both are subject to assumptions and artifacts [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5].

The general activation-agent literature shows that **KOH is associated with highly microporous materials**, while physical activation with oxidizing gases like CO₂ favors microporosity at the expense of mesopores and macropores [N2-F3]. By contrast, steam-activated carbons are associated with lower micropore content and more mesopore/macropore development [N2-F3].
